theoryOfChange: The Cancer Research Institute (CRI) describes its strategic approach in its annual impact reports. The '2024 Impact Report' highlights the organization's 'People x Biology x Data' strategy as an 'innovative framework' that integrates bioinformatics, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning to advance cancer immunotherapy. This framework aims to enhance researchers' ability to analyze complex biological data, identify novel biomarkers, and develop personalized treatment strategies, thereby accelerating the pace of discovery and ensuring new insights are translated into effective therapies for patients. The report also refers to this as a 'cohesive strategy to advance cancer immunotherapy, turning bold ideas into real-world impact.'

rich_narrative.summary: The Cancer Research Institute (CRI) is a global leader in the field of immunotherapy, dedicated to harnessing the immune system to conquer all forms of cancer. <cite id="1">founded in 1953</cite>, the organization has spent decades funding the laboratory and clinical research necessary to bring life-saving treatments to patients. In FY2024, CRI reported <cite id="2">total revenue of $23,964,638</cite>, representing a <cite id="3">26% decline from the previous fiscal year</cite>. Despite this recent dip in funding, the organization maintains a <cite id="4">94/100 rating from Charity Navigator</cite>, reflecting high standards of accountability and financial health. The institute's primary mechanism for impact is its grantmaking, which supports <cite id="5">clinician-scientists launching innovative phase I/II clinical studies</cite>. In FY2023, CRI awarded <cite id="6">73 new research grants</cite> and committed <cite id="7">$28.7 million in new research funding</cite>. While the organization operates globally, its spending is concentrated in the United States, with <cite id="8">$40.8 million in domestic grants</cite> compared to <cite id="9">$9.4 million in foreign grants</cite>. This focus on systemic change through high-level research means that while the cost-per-beneficiary is low, the time horizon for clinical results is often measured in years rather than months.
